claims.claim: The model card format comes from Mitchell et al. (2019), Model Cards for Model Reporting.
claims.source: Mitchell et al., Proceedings of FAT* 2019, pages 220 to 229.

concept_html:
A model card is a short document that travels with a model. It tells users what the model is for, how well it works, for whom, and where it should not be used. The format comes from Mitchell et al., "Model Cards for Model Reporting" (2019). Keep it in the repository next to the training code, and link it from the registered model version (lesson B14-L2).

Sections to include:

  • Model details: name, version, registry alias, owners, training date, run ID.
  • Intended use: the decision it supports and who uses it.
  • Out-of-scope uses: uses it must not serve, stated plainly.
  • Training data: source, period, grain, known gaps.
  • Evaluation: the honest metric (lesson B11-L3), with the test period and prevalence.
  • Subgroup results: rates per group with counts (lesson B13-L3), including the weakest group.
  • Limitations and risks: known failure modes, drift risks, proxies.
  • Monitoring and review: what is tracked, alert thresholds, next review date.

Write numbers with their context: "AUC 0.78 on October to December 2026 customers, 2.4% positive rate, 51,000 rows". A bare "AUC 0.78" invites misuse.

State limits as clearly as strengths. "Recall for customers over 70 is 0.28 against 0.62 overall. Do not use for outreach targeting of this group without human review" protects the people affected and the team that built the model.

Treat the card as code: a template with required sections, reviewed in the same pull request as the model change. A check in CI can refuse a card with missing sections.

lines: Model details: churn_model v4 (@champion), owner Retention Analytics, run 4da8..., trained 2026-09-01
Intended use: rank active customers for the monthly retention call list (top 500)
Out of scope: credit, collections or pricing decisions; customers with under 3 months' tenure
Training data: CRM extract Jan 2024 to Jun 2026, one row per customer-month
Evaluation: AUC 0.78, average precision 0.21 (prevalence 2.4%), test Oct to Dec 2026, 51,000 rows
Subgroups: recall at top 500 is 0.62 overall, 0.28 for customers over 70 (n positives = 64)
Limitations: sparse digital activity lowers recall for older customers; tenure proxies contract type
Monitoring: monthly AUC and calibration, alert below 0.72; next review 2027-03-01

exercises.prompt: Write `missing_sections(card: dict[str, str], required: list[str]) -> list[str]`. Return the required section names, in the order of `required`, that are absent from `card` or contain only whitespace. CI will fail the build when the list is not empty.
exercises.prompt_html: Write missing_sections(card: dict[str, str], required: list[str]) -> list[str]. Return the required section names, in the order of required, that are absent from card or contain only whitespace. CI will fail the build when the list is not empty.
exercises.solution:
def missing_sections(card: dict[str, str], required: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Required model card sections that are absent or blank.

    Args:
        card: Section name to text.
        required: Section names that must have content.

    Returns:
        Missing section names, in the order of required.
    """
    return [name for name in required if not card.get(name, "").strip()]

title: Model cards that state limits as clearly as scores
why_html: A propensity model built for marketing emails was later reused by another team to prioritise collections calls. Nobody had written down that it was trained only on customers who had opted in to marketing, a group with very different payment behaviour. Collections priorities were wrong for months. An "Out-of-scope uses" line, "Not validated for credit or collections decisions", would have stopped the reuse at the first review.
